newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Nikkei's drop defies ratio analysis - experts.
newsitem.headline: Japan Nikkei's drop defies ratio analysis - experts.

text.p: Although Japanese stocks currently show nearly triple the investment value of high-flying U.S. stocks, such ratios do not reflect the realities of the convuluted Japanese accounting system, analysts say.

According to Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics data, the price earnings ratio (PER) of the key Nikkei 225 average stood between 46 to 60 times, compared with 20 times in the United States.
The P/E ratio -- the price of a stock divided by earnings per share -- is the yardstick used to measure a company's earning power and investment value.

"Japan stocks have fallen considerably lately and from a historical cash flow point of view, they are falling into the range where they are far from being overvalued," said Tim Hayashida, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
"But differences in accounting make comparisons on a PER basis difficult," he added.

Japanese firms' balance sheets are traditionally based on purchase prices, which means the older the company, the lower the value of its assets, compared with their current market value, analysts said.
Current Japanese accounting rules require firms to disclose the financial statement of a subsidiary only if 50 percent of the unit's shares are owned by the parent firm.
Strategists agreed that it was unfair to judge Japanese firms from a global point of view when their profits are expressed in domestic forms.
But they said the issues currently being sought were mainly those which adhered to global standards.

"The market is clearly divided between internationally competitive issues and those which have unclear financial structures -- such as the banking and construction sectors, which are saddled with bad loans," said Tetsuya Murakami, a strategist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

"The double-tiered state of the market will probably continue in the coming months as the stock market struggles to get back on its feet and cautious investors scrutinise what they are planning to buy more carefully," he said.

New international accounting standards being considered to bring Japanese companies more in line with foreign counterparts will force disclosure of all of their group earnings if they are involved in the management of a subsidiary, analysts said.

Morgan Stanley's chief global strategist Barton Biggs said in a lecture on Tuesday that stock prices were "reasonable" when compared with the yield of government bonds, although the the profitability of Japanese firms at present was not good.

With the price book-value ratio (PBR) of Japanese stocks -- another key yardstick to evaluate stock levels -- falling to just below two times, the shares cannot be called undervalued by international standards but are reasonably priced given their historical performance in Japan, he said.
